pairs.rationale: Both sayings announce that the hour has come and connect it with the Son's glorification. John 12 names the Son of Man's glorification; the prayer asks the Father to glorify the Son so the Son may glorify the Father. The earlier announcement and later petition remain distinct speeches.

Both passages connect the Father's grant to the Son with authority and the giving of life. John 5 also specifies judgment and life in Himself, while the prayer gives authority over all flesh and life to those the Father gives. The different scopes and purposes are retained rather than making every authority statement an identical promise.

Both passages join knowing the true God with Jesus Christ and eternal life. The prayer expressly addresses the Father and identifies Jesus Christ as His sent One; the epistle speaks of knowing the True One and being in His Son. The comparison preserves the clauses rather than newly deciding an ambiguous pronoun's antecedent.

Jesus earlier describes His food as doing His Sender's will and completing His work; the prayer says He glorified the Father by completing the work given Him. This is the same Father-given-work motif expressed as mission and completion, without deleting the still-forthcoming passion or the later It is finished saying.

The prayer speaks of the glory Jesus had with the Father before the world's existence; the prologue places the Word with God in the beginning and creation through Him. Both locate His relation to God before the created world. The prayer's glory petition is additional rather than a word-for-word repetition of the prologue.

The prayer later returns explicitly to making the Father's name known to the disciples and its continuing purpose in love and indwelling. That recalls this earlier revealed-name statement within the same prayer. It is an internal recurrence, not a claim about a newly reconstructed pronunciation of the divine name or another independent revelation.

The disciples have just said now we know and affirmed Jesus' coming from God; Jesus now presents their recognition that His gifts come from the Father. The connection is their acknowledged understanding in the immediate farewell setting. It does not turn their knowledge into perfect comprehension of everything, especially given the following warning about scattering.

The prayer says the disciples received the given words and believed Jesus came forth from and was sent by the Father. The earlier discourse says they believed He came forth from God and explicitly describes His coming from the Father into the world. The comparison preserves received testimony and the Sender-Son relationship.

Jesus prays specifically for the disciples given Him; Luke records His prayer that Peter's faith not fail amid Satan's demand to sift the group. Both portray intercession for threatened followers. The group versus Peter focus differs, and this particular prayer's not-for-the-world clause is not made a statement that Jesus never seeks the world's salvation.

The prayer declares the mutual belonging of the Father's and Son's things and Jesus' glorification in the disciples; the preceding discourse says everything the Father has is His and the Spirit will glorify Him by declaring what is His. The repeated possession-and-glory language retains the different roles of Spirit and disciples.

The prayer asks the Father to preserve the disciples and seeks their oneness according to Father and Son; John 10 speaks of preservation from snatching in the Son's and Father's hands and says they are one. The shared preservation-and-unity language does not change the prayer's name-given-to-the-Son wording or equate all kinds of unity without qualification.

The prayer's exception among the guarded disciples is compared with Jesus' earlier warning that one of the chosen Twelve is a devil, explicitly identified as Judas who would hand Him over. This illuminates the betrayal exception in its narrative context without asserting Judas was already physically dead when the prayer was spoken.

Both statements explain Jesus' speaking as directed toward His joy being within the disciples and their joy being made full. The earlier farewell instruction and later prayer repeat this specific purpose, with the prayer additionally expressing His coming to the Father.

The prayer joins the given word with the world's hatred and the disciples' not being from the world; the farewell teaching explicitly says the world hates them because Jesus chose them out of it and had hated Him first. The comparison retains the disciples' relation to their Master rather than inventing a separate origin story.

Both prayers ask God for protection or deliverance from evil. The Lord's Prayer says deliver us from evil, while John says keep them from the evil one and expressly distinguishes preservation from removal out of the world. The supplied evil and evil-one forms are not silently made identical.

Both passages expressly describe the disciples as not from the world. John 15 explains that Jesus chose them out of the world; the prayer relates their position to His own. This is a repeated belonging-and-allegiance statement, not an assertion that the disciples share every feature of Jesus' heavenly preexistence.

The prayer calls the Father's word truth; the actual Greek-OT psalm says the beginning of His words is truth and His righteous judgments endure. This is a specific divine-word-and-truth comparison, with sanctifying the disciples as the prayer's additional petition and the exact Psalm numbering retained.

The Father-sends-Jesus and Jesus-sends-disciples pattern is explicitly repeated after the resurrection. The prayer speaks of sending them into the world, while the later appearance directly commissions the hearers. The earlier prayer and later risen-Jesus commission retain their order and wording.

Jesus dedicates Himself for the disciples' sanctification; Hebrews explains sanctification through the offering of Jesus Christ's body according to God's will. The shared relation is His self-giving for others' sanctification. John frames it in truth, while Hebrews expressly describes the once-for-all bodily offering rather than using identical wording.

Jesus extends His prayer to believers reached through the disciples' word; Romans connects believing with hearing and hearing with sent proclamation and Christ's word. Both describe faith mediated through communicated testimony. Romans also says not all obey, so the connection does not turn every hearer into a believer.

The prayer seeks believers' oneness in relation to Father and Son, with witness to the world; Ephesians urges unity of the Spirit and names one body, Spirit, hope, Lord, faith, baptism and God and Father. Both ground communal unity in divine relation, with the prayer's mutual-indwelling and mission clauses remaining distinct.

Jesus describes giving the disciples received glory for their unity; Paul describes believers beholding the Lord's glory and being transformed from glory to glory through the Spirit. Both concern believers' participation in glory. Giving for unity and transformation into an image are distinct expressions, not interchangeable accounts of one event.

The prayer's I in them and Thou in Me corresponds to the earlier I in My Father, you in Me and I in you, joined with the Father's love for Jesus' followers. The mutual-relation and love motifs recur, while the later prayer additionally gives unity and the world's recognition as purposes.

The prayer desires that those given Him be with Him where He is and behold His glory; the earlier promise says He prepares a place and will take the disciples to Himself so they may be where He is. The shared with-Me-where-I-am promise does not supply a new timetable or replace the prayer's before-the-world love clause.

Both passages contrast others' failure to know the Father with Jesus' knowledge of Him. John 8 addresses particular opponents and also speaks of the Father's glorifying Jesus, while the prayer speaks of the world and the disciples' recognition of His sending. Those different audiences and scopes remain visible.

The prayer seeks the Father's love for the Son within the disciples and Jesus in them; the earlier discourse says the Father's love for Jesus is extended through Jesus' love to them and calls them to remain in it. This is the recurring Father-Son-disciples love relation, not another narrated visit or a new set of speakers.

Both accounts move Jesus and the disciples to the place of the ensuing arrest. John specifies a garden beyond the winter-stream Kidron; Mark names Gethsemane and introduces prayer there. The descriptions are compared without replacing John's geographical wording or inserting Mark's place-name into John's actual text.

Judas knows the place because Jesus often gathered there with the disciples; Luke describes Jesus' customary journey to the Mount of Olives with disciples following. The recurring practice illuminates the familiarity of the setting, without making Luke independently state Judas's knowledge or the garden's precise location.

Judas arrives with an armed group in both accounts. John specifies a cohort and officers associated with chief priests and Pharisees, plus lights and weapons; Mark names a sword-and-club crowd from chief priests, scribes and elders. The different group descriptions are retained without estimating troop numbers or adding a narrated kiss to John.

Jesus knowingly steps forward to meet the arrest party; His earlier saying explains that He lays down His life of His own accord under the Father's command. The action is compared with the teaching about voluntary self-giving, without making the encounter a denial that others arrest Him or adding a mechanism for His foreknowledge.

Jesus' I am answer to the requested identity is explicitly recalled by I told you that I am when He asks that the disciples be allowed to leave. This is a repeated self-identification within the arrest encounter, not a claim that the ordinary identity question alone proves a separately reconstructed divine-name quotation.

The arrest party goes backward and falls when Jesus speaks; the psalm describes enemies approaching to consume the righteous speaker, growing weak and falling. The concrete approach-and-fall pattern is compared without asserting an explicit Psalm quotation, identical enemies, or a physical mechanism beyond what John narrates.

John explicitly repeats Jesus' question Whom do you seek and the party's Jesus-the-Nazarene answer after the first exchange and the fall. The matched question-and-answer sequence is an internal narrative repetition. It does not exchange the speakers or collapse the repeated stages into a single utterance.

Jesus offers Himself as the sought person while asking that His followers go; His shepherd teaching contrasts laying down His life for the sheep with abandoning them to danger. The arrest action illustrates concern for followers within His self-giving. It does not turn the armed party into the literal wolf of the figure.

The narrator relates the disciples' preservation to Jesus' lost-not-one word about those given by the Father. John 6 similarly promises losing nothing given Him and raising it on the last day. The immediate protection at arrest and the broader life-and-resurrection promise remain distinct scopes rather than a new verbatim harmonized quotation.

Both accounts identify the high priest's slave's right ear as cut off. John names Peter as the swordsman and Malchus as the slave; Luke leaves them unnamed and expressly narrates Jesus' healing the ear. The shared injury does not add Luke's healing sentence to John or remove John's names.

Jesus commands the sword returned in both arrest accounts. John addresses Peter and speaks of the Father's cup; Matthew addresses the unnamed swordsman and adds the sword warning, available angelic aid and Scripture's fulfillment. The close rebuke parallel preserves those different explanations.

John's Jesus accepts the cup the Father gives Him; Mark's earlier prayer asks the Father that the cup be removed while submitting to His will. These are complementary cup-and-Father sayings at different stages, not the same speech or a claim that John records the earlier prayer.

Both accounts narrate Jesus being seized. John additionally identifies the cohort, commander and officers and explicitly says He is bound; Mark's immediate sentence simply says they lay hands on and seize Him. The link does not import John's military titles or immediate binding into Mark's sentence.

John names Annas and Caiaphas in explaining the first destination and their family relation; Luke names both in its high-priesthood dating notice. The comparison supplies a specific shared priestly setting, not independent confirmation of the father-in-law relation, the first Annas hearing or an identical legal-office arrangement at every date.

John explicitly recalls Caiaphas's earlier advice that one person should die for the people. The earlier scene gives the statement and the narrator's further interpretation about gathering God's scattered children. This is a direct retrospective speech reference rather than an independent repetition of the original council meeting.

Peter follows Jesus into the high-priestly courtyard setting in both accounts. John distinguishes another disciple who enters first because he is known there, with Peter initially outside; Matthew says Peter follows at a distance and enters to sit with the officers. John's unnamed other disciple is not assigned a personal name by this parallel.

A servant girl associates Peter with Jesus and Peter denies it in both accounts. John identifies her as the doorkeeper and records I am not; Matthew places the challenge in the courtyard and gives I do not know what you are saying. Location, question form and denial wording remain distinct.

Both passages place Peter with the attendants or officers warming at a fire in the high priest's courtyard. John specifies charcoal, cold weather and standing; Mark says Peter sits and warms at the firelight. The comparison preserves the recorded posture and descriptions without inventing a shared moment or change of position.

Both passages give high-priestly questioning of Jesus, but John asks about His disciples and teaching, whereas Matthew asks about testimony and His messianic sonship. Their different questions and responses are compared as religious-hearing scenes, without making a single transcript or moving John's Annas-to-Caiaphas sequence.

Jesus appeals to His publicly accessible temple teaching in both scenes. Mark places the statement at arrest, emphasizing daily teaching without seizure; John places it in the hearing, also naming synagogues and denying secret teaching. The close public-teaching defense keeps its different occasions and additional clauses.

Jesus asks that those who heard His teaching be questioned; Nicodemus earlier challenges judgment without hearing a person and knowing what he does. Both demand informed hearing rather than unsupported judgment, but questioning hearers and hearing the accused are distinct applications. No additional historical trial-law ruling is inferred.

John narrates an officer slapping Jesus after His answer to the high priest; Mark records attendants receiving Him with slaps after other abuse in the hearing. The shared physical mistreatment does not merge the stated triggers or add Mark's blindfolding, spitting or fists to John's specific slap.

Jesus challenges being struck if His speech is right; Paul protests an ordered mouth-blow while being judged according to law. Both hearing scenes join a blow with a challenge about its justification. Jesus' conditional appeal and Paul's sharp reply, subsequent explanation and named high priest are different and are not treated as one response.

John says Annas sends Jesus bound to Caiaphas; Matthew says those who seize Jesus lead Him to Caiaphas where scribes and elders gather. The shared Caiaphas destination is retained, while Matthew does not narrate John's prior Annas stage and the texts are not reordered to erase that difference.

Both accounts narrate a further accusation and denial by Peter. John keeps him warming and records a plural challenge with I am not; Matthew places a second girl's statement at the gateway and adds an oath denying knowledge of the Man. The accusers, position and denial wording remain as given.

The accuser is expressly described as a relative of the slave whose ear Peter cut off, pointing back to the named Malchus episode. This direct internal reference clarifies why the garden encounter matters. It does not identify the relative as Malchus himself or supply his personal name.

Peter's further denial is followed immediately by the rooster, fulfilling the earlier prediction of three denials before it crows. This is an explicit forecast-and-event relationship within John. It does not import Mark's two-crow wording or another Gospel's look and tears into John's account.

Both accounts narrate the early-morning movement from the religious hearing to Pilate. John names the praetorium and the accusers' purification concern; Mark names the consultation and binding before delivery. These compare the transfer without resolving Passover-meal chronology or moving John's earlier binding to Mark's narrated point.

John's Pilate asks the charge after the accusers bring Jesus; Luke narrates their bringing Him and states their accusations. Luke supplies a related recorded charge scene rather than a verbatim answer to John's particular question, and the allegations are not thereby endorsed as facts.

John's accusers justify delivery by alleging wrongdoing; Luke specifies allegations about the nation, tribute and a royal claim. The shared prosecutorial setting is compared while preserving John's nonspecific answer. In particular, the tribute allegation remains the accusers' statement, not a narrator's finding that Jesus forbade payment.

The exchange about judging Jesus under the accusers' law and their stated lack of death authority recurs in a changed form when Pilate tells them to take and crucify Him and they invoke their law. This is an internal legal-claim contrast, not a newly reconstructed uniform rule about historical execution powers.

John earlier explicitly explains Jesus' lifted-up saying as indicating the kind of death He would die; the trial narrative now explicitly invokes fulfillment of His saying about that kind of death. The matching narrative explanation links the prediction and passion setting without adding a new chronology or execution method.

Pilate asks Jesus whether He is King of the Jews in both passages. Mark immediately gives You say so, while John develops a longer exchange before its royal response. The matching interrogation does not flatten John's intervening questions into Mark's shorter form.

Pilate refers to Jesus' own nation and chief priests delivering Him and asks His deed; Mark narrates delivery by the assembled leaders and ensuing accusations by chief priests. The common delivery-and-charge setting does not assign every member of the nation an identical role or add Mark's wording to Pilate's question.

Jesus says His kingdom does not originate from this world or depend on fighting attendants; earlier He withdraws when people intend to seize Him and make Him king. Both passages distinguish His kingship from a humanly imposed or force-secured rule. They do not deny His kingship or assert that His mission has no earthly consequences.

Jesus explains before Pilate that He came to bear witness to the truth; the epistle expressly recalls Christ Jesus testifying the good confession before Pontius Pilate. This is a concrete canonical reference to the same witness setting, without claiming the epistle reproduces every royal or truth clause of John's dialogue.

Both passages record Pilate declaring that he finds no charge or ground for a charge against Jesus. John places the verdict after the distinctive What is truth question; Luke addresses the chief priests and crowds without that question. The matching finding does not insert John's preceding dialogue into Luke.

Both accounts describe a festival prisoner-release custom and Pilate's proposal to release the King of the Jews. Mark adds the crowd's request and a description of Barabbas's company. This is a comparison of the supplied narrative notices, not external confirmation of the custom's historical scope.

Both accounts record the demand for Barabbas rather than Jesus. John calls him a bandit; Luke describes his imprisonment for an uprising and murder. The different narrator descriptions remain explicit, while the crowd's demand is not confused with Pilate's proposed release of Jesus.

Both accounts attribute Jesus' scourging to Pilate's action. Mark includes it with the prisoner release and delivery for crucifixion; John narrates it before the further public exchanges and final delivery. The comparison preserves those narrative placements rather than positing an unrecorded second scourging to reconcile them.

Both passages describe the soldiers' purple clothing of Jesus and a woven crown of thorns. John specifies placement on His head and Mark gives the order in its own sentence. These close mocking-costume details are retained without adding other accounts' garments or actions.

The soldiers salute Jesus as King of the Jews and mistreat Him in both accounts. John records slaps and their repeated approach; Mark records a reed striking His head, spitting and kneeling. The matching mock-royal address does not make the different physical acts identical.

Pilate again declares no charge against Jesus in John and says his examination found no ground for the accusers' charges in Luke. John adds the plan to bring Jesus outside. The repeated innocence finding is compared without importing every detail of one public speech into the other.

Both accounts describe Jesus in a thorn crown and a mocking garment. John presents Him outside in purple with Behold the Man; Matthew describes a scarlet cloak, the soldiers' mockery, then its removal before departure. Color descriptions, speakers and the public-presentation versus removal stages are preserved without a textile or timeline harmonization.

Both passages join repeated cries for crucifixion with Pilate's claim that he finds no ground for a capital charge. John identifies chief priests and officers at this point and adds Take Him yourselves; Luke gives the third protest and a proposed punishment-and-release. The speaker groups and proposals remain as narrated.

John's accusers invoke their law and a death penalty because of Jesus' claimed sonship; Matthew's religious hearing proceeds from the Christ-and-Son-of-God question to a blasphemy charge and liability to death. The connection concerns the stated accusations and judgments, not an endorsement that Jesus' sonship is false or a new legal ruling.

Both accounts narrate Jesus giving Pilate no answer at a particular stage. John's question is Where art Thou from; Mark's concerns the many accusations and adds Pilate's amazement. The bounded silences are compared without claiming Jesus never speaks to Pilate or combining their different questions.

Pilate claims authority to release or crucify Jesus; Jesus earlier claims Father-commanded authority over laying down and taking up His own life. The same life-and-authority subject exposes different kinds of claims: a governor's judicial choice and Jesus' self-giving and resurrection. Neither claim is silently substituted for the other.

Jesus denies that Pilate has authority independent of a grant from above; Romans says existing authorities derive from God. The specific comparison is the divine derivation of authority, not approval of every exercise of it. John's greater-sin comparison remains, and this unit does not name the other hander-over.

Both accusation scenes frame Jesus' royal identity as a matter involving Caesar. John gives the pressure that releasing such a king opposes Caesar; Luke records charges about tribute and being Christ, a king. These are the accusers' political claims, not narrator findings that Jesus forbade tribute or unlawfully seized rule.

Both narratives place Pilate on the judgment seat during Jesus' case. John names the Stone Pavement and Gabbatha; Matthew gives his wife's message at that point in its account. The shared judicial setting does not add the wife's dream to John or independently locate the named pavement.

Both supply explicit passion-hour notices, but they differ: John gives about the sixth hour for Pilate's presentation on the Preparation of Passover, while Mark gives the third hour for crucifixion. This compares the notices with their distinct events and expressions; it does not invent a clock conversion or identify them as the same moment.

The cries for crucifixion and Pilate's continued questioning recur in both accounts. John additionally records his royal question and the chief priests' no-king-except-Caesar reply; Mark asks what evil Jesus has done. The shared demand does not erase the different dialogue or transfer John's explicit chief-priest answer to an undifferentiated whole people.

Both passages conclude the proceeding with Jesus handed over to the demanded outcome. Luke explicitly pairs this with release of the uprising-and-murder prisoner; John moves directly into Jesus being taken for crucifixion. The matching delivery is retained without assigning every subsequent action to the same unnamed group.

Both accounts reach Golgotha, the Place of a Skull, but identify cross-carrying differently: John says Jesus bears it for Himself, while Mark compels Simon of Cyrene. The shared destination and carrying motif are compared without inventing the point of a handoff or replacing either named carrier.

Both accounts place two others alongside Jesus in the crucifixion, one on each side. Luke explicitly calls them criminals and names the Skull location; John calls them two others and places Jesus in the middle. Those narrator descriptions remain distinct rather than supplying every Gospel with the same label.

Both record a royal charge over Jesus' cross, but John gives Jesus the Nazarene, the King of the Jews and attributes the writing to Pilate; Matthew gives This is Jesus, the King of the Jews. The close inscription parallel preserves the actual title forms and each account's additional placement or authorship detail.

Both passages concern the inscription above the crucified Jesus. John additionally gives its many readers, nearness to the city and Hebrew, Latin and Greek wording; this supplied Luke unit simply gives the royal inscription. It does not independently attest the three languages or allow their restoration from another edition.

The chief priests want the placard recast as Jesus' self-claim to kingship; the recorded exchange with Pilate gives Jesus' You say that I am a king and His truth-witness explanation. Comparing the actual speech with the proposed wording distinguishes the accusers' formulation from a verbatim transcript of Jesus' answer.

Both passages narrate the soldiers' division of Jesus' clothing. John distinguishes four parts and a separate seamless tunic, with the lot decision following; Mark summarizes division by lots. The comparison preserves garments and tunic as John distinguishes them, rather than treating every item as one undivided robe.

John explicitly quotes Scripture about divided garments and a lot for clothing; the actual Greek-OT Psalm unit gives both actions in closely matching words. The fulfillment citation is anchored to its supplied Psalm ID, while John's specific tunic decision remains the narrative application rather than an added detail in the psalm.

Mary Magdalene appears among the women in both crucifixion accounts. John places the named women beside the cross and includes Jesus' mother and her sister; Mark describes women watching from a distance with a different list. Their positions and names are preserved without identifying the unnamed sister with Salome or equating different Mary descriptions.

The disciple whom Jesus loved appears at the cross; the supper narrative earlier introduces a disciple with that same identifying description reclining near Jesus. This links the recurring unnamed figure without assigning a personal name or deriving his identity merely from later tradition. The mother's new-son charge remains additional here.

The two sayings form explicit complementary directions: Jesus tells His mother behold your son, then tells the disciple behold your mother. This is an internal reciprocal charge followed here by home care, not independent testimony or a separately established legal adoption ceremony.

The psalm describes thirst met with sour wine; John links Jesus' I thirst with Scripture's completion and then narrates the sour wine. The concrete thirst-and-drink relation is compared using the actual Greek-OT ID. The psalm's additional gall for food is not inserted into John's scene.

Both passages describe a sour-wine-filled sponge brought to Jesus. John gives a vessel and hyssop; Mark places it on a reed and adds the Elijah remark. Implements and accompanying speech remain distinct, and this drink is not confused with an earlier offered mixture that another scene says He refused.

Both narrate Jesus' death in connection with His final speech and spirit. John gives It is finished, the bowed head and giving up His spirit; Luke gives the loud Father-into-Thy-hands prayer and breathing His last. The different recorded sayings and actions are not assembled into an unprovided sequence of last words.

John explains the request that bodies not remain on the crosses over the Sabbath; Deuteronomy forbids leaving a hanged body overnight and commands burial that day. The body-removal concern has concrete legal background, while John adds the great Sabbath and the leg-breaking request, neither of which the law itself prescribes here.

The narrative explicitly contrasts the soldiers' breaking the two others' legs with not breaking Jesus' legs because He is already dead. This is a deliberate adjacent difference in treatment and its stated reason, not a claim about an unreported exact death time for the other men.

The later narrator explicitly interprets Jesus' unbroken bones as Scripture's fulfillment. It points back to the soldiers' decision not to break His legs after finding Him dead. This is an action-and-scriptural-explanation link within the same account, with no added leg-breaking or additional injury.

John narrates blood and water from Jesus' pierced side and immediately appeals to witness; the epistle joins Jesus Christ with water, blood and the Spirit's testimony. The distinctive water-blood-witness cluster is compared without asserting that the epistle explicitly describes this wound or determines a medical or sacramental explanation of its fluids.

Both narrator statements affirm true testimony: one concerns the person who saw and testifies so others may believe, the other the disciple who testifies and wrote these things, with we know. The recurring witness formula does not by itself establish an additional personal name or a new theory about the plural voice.

John presents the unbroken bone as Scripture fulfilled; the Passover law specifically forbids breaking a bone of the animal eaten. This is concrete possible Passover-scripture background, with the command's you-shall-not-break wording and John's passive fulfillment wording preserved rather than claimed as a verbatim or uniquely identified citation.

The actual psalm says the Lord guards all their bones and not one will be shattered; John cites the unbroken bone of His as fulfillment. The shared protection-from-breaking form supplies another possible scriptural connection, while the psalm's plural righteous and John's singular application remain distinct.

John's Scripture wording is look on the One whom they pierced. The supplied Zechariah says look toward Me because they danced in mockery and adds mourning over a beloved one and firstborn. The prophetic looking-and-mistreatment context is compared as possible citation background with an explicit wording difference, not a verbatim match or a replacement of mockery with pierced.

Both accounts name Joseph of Arimathea asking Pilate for Jesus' body and receiving permission. John calls him a secret disciple because of fear; Mark describes his daring approach, council standing and Pilate's inquiry. Those different descriptions are retained without inventing a new prior biography or making the public request erase the narrated fear.

John expressly identifies Nicodemus here as the man who first came to Jesus by night, matching the earlier named visit. This is a direct retrospective person-and-visit reference. The myrrh, aloes and hundred-litrai quantity remain particular to the burial scene rather than being added to his earlier conversation.

Both accounts describe Jesus' body wrapped in linen for burial. John uses a plural subject after Joseph and Nicodemus and adds cloths with spices and the burial custom; Luke narrates Joseph's wrapping in linen before placement. The agents and the spice detail remain as given rather than being supplied to every account.

Both passages specify a tomb in which no one had yet been laid. John additionally locates the new tomb in a garden near the crucifixion; Luke describes a rock-cut tomb. The unused-tomb correspondence does not independently confirm John's garden layout or erase the different architectural descriptions.

Both accounts connect Jesus' burial with Preparation and the approaching Sabbath. John expressly gives the tomb's nearness as the reason for using it; Luke states the day's designation and Sabbath's beginning after describing the burial. The shared scheduling context does not invent an extra travel route or harmonized clock.

Both accounts place a tomb visit early on the first day of the week and describe the stone already moved. John focuses on Mary Magdalene while it is still dark; Mark's preceding list gives several women and says the sun has risen. Group and light descriptions are retained without inventing separate departure and arrival times to reconcile them.

Both accounts connect a women's tomb report with Peter's movement to inspect it. John's initial report to Peter and the beloved disciple says the body was taken and its location unknown; Luke's group reports the preceding tomb message to the Eleven and others. The first report is not silently turned into Mary's later I-have-seen-the-Lord announcement.

Both passages narrate Peter going to the tomb after the report. John explicitly includes the other disciple and subsequently distinguishes their movements; Luke names Peter running and inspecting the linen. The shared Peter journey does not add or deny an unnamed companion in Luke's shorter sentence.

The later entry statement explicitly recalls the other disciple as the one who came to the tomb first, pointing back to his outrunning Peter. This is a direct internal arrival reference. John still gives Peter the first narrated entry, so arriving first and entering first are not assigned to the same person.

Both accounts describe stooping to inspect the tomb and seeing linen cloths, but John initially assigns that look without entry to the other disciple, while Luke assigns the stooping to Peter. The matching action is compared with its different named or unnamed agent rather than exchanging their roles.

Peter sees the linen cloths at the tomb in both accounts. John expressly narrates his entering after the other disciple arrives; Luke says he stoops to look and then departs in wonder. The comparison preserves John's explicit entry and does not manufacture an entry sentence or shared race order in Luke.

Both resurrection scenes identify a face cloth along with bodily linen wrappings. Lazarus comes out still bound and must be unbound; Jesus' face cloth is separate from the lying linen cloths in the empty tomb. The different persons and arrangements remain, with no invented folded-napkin custom or physical mechanism of resurrection.

Both narrator statements connect the resurrection setting with belief. The earlier forward-looking notice says the disciples remember and believe the Scripture and Jesus' word after His rising; here the other disciple sees and believes before the following not-yet-Scripture-knowledge statement. The unstated object and extent of this first belief are not filled in as complete scriptural understanding.

John states that the disciples did not yet know the Scripture about His necessary rising; Luke later narrates Jesus opening the disciples' minds to Scripture and explaining the Messiah's suffering and third-day rising. The knowledge-and-Scripture connection preserves the differing stages and does not identify an Old Testament verse John himself leaves unnamed.

Both accounts end the tomb inspection with departure. John specifies the disciples returning to their own place without adding an emotional description here; Luke narrates Peter going away while wondering. The shared departure does not add John's stated destination to Luke or transfer Luke's reaction to both of John's disciples.

Mary's weeping while looking into the tomb is explicitly addressed by the angels' subsequent Why do you weep and her answer about the missing body. This is an internal explanation of the grief narrated here. Her assumption about removal remains her report rather than the narrator's explanation of the empty tomb.

Both tomb scenes introduce two white or radiant figures addressing women. John calls them angels seated at the head and feet of the former body-place; Luke introduces men standing in flashing clothing and the women bow. Their descriptions, positions, questions and audiences remain distinct rather than a combined stage direction.

Mary repeats her earlier body-removal report and uncertainty about its location, now to the angels rather than to Peter and the other disciple. John changes we do not know to I do not know and the Lord to my Lord. The explicit recurrence keeps those pronouns and remains a character's mistaken assumption, not a narrator finding of theft.

Both accounts describe the risen Jesus present with followers who do not initially recognize Him. Luke expressly says the travelers' eyes were held back; John simply reports Mary's failure to know Him. Luke's cause is not imposed on John, nor are the tomb garden and Emmaus road treated as one encounter.

Jesus repeats the angels' Woman, why do you weep question and adds Whom do you seek. Mary again responds from the assumption of a removed body, now supposing a gardener. This is a deliberate question-and-misunderstanding recurrence, not an identification of the angels with Jesus or narrator approval of the gardener assumption.

Jesus' personal Mary call leads to recognition; the shepherd figure describes calling his own sheep by name and their knowing his voice. The scene provides a concrete illustration of personal call and recognition, without claiming John explicitly quotes the earlier figure or explains the cause of Mary's previous nonrecognition.

Both passages give women a message for Jesus' brothers after meeting Him. Matthew narrates grasped feet, worship and a Galilee instruction; John records Do not cling and the Father-and-God ascent message. John's command is not turned into a separately narrated completed act of clinging, and the different messages and contact descriptions remain.

Both supplied texts describe Mary Magdalene reporting that she has seen the risen Jesus. John's report includes His message; Mark's bracketed longer ending adds the recipients' mourning and unbelief and its own first-appearance statement. These are compared as supplied without adding those details to John or giving the longer ending fresh critical-text approval.

Both passages describe Jesus standing among the disciples and offering peace. John adds the first-day evening, shut doors and fear context; Luke places the appearance amid the gathered group's discussion. Those details remain distinct, with John's later explicit Thomas absence not erased by assumptions about Luke's collective group label.

Both risen-Jesus scenes show bodily evidence and joy among the followers. John names hands and side, with rejoicing at seeing the Lord; Luke names hands and feet and describes continuing disbelief for joy. Body parts and stated responses are preserved rather than making John's side wound into Luke's feet or all joy identical belief.

The risen Jesus repeats the Father-sent-Me and I-send-you relation already spoken in the prayer. The prayer describes sending into the world; the appearance directly addresses and commissions the disciples with peace. The recurring mission formula keeps its earlier prayer and later appearance settings.

Jesus breathes and commands reception of the Holy Spirit; Genesis depicts God breathing life's breath into the formed human. This is a possible creative-breath image connecting life-giving actions, not a claim that Genesis itself names the Holy Spirit here or that the bodily formation and risen-Jesus scene are one act.

Jesus gives a consequential forgiving-and-retaining charge; Matthew gives a binding-and-loosing charge with earthly and heavenly correspondence. The comparison concerns delegated responsibility and its stated consequences. It does not make the different verbs identical definitions or settle every later account of the scope and manner of that responsibility.

Both passages identify Thomas with the explicit name Didymus. The earlier account gives his words about going with Jesus, whereas this one records his absence from the first group appearance. The recurring-person reference does not reconstruct his reason for absence or make one statement describe his permanent attitude.

Jesus later explicitly answers Thomas's requested hand-and-side tests with corresponding invitations and a call from unbelief to belief. This is a stated-demand and offered-response relationship, preserving finger, hand, nail marks and side. Neither verse states that Thomas actually performs the proposed touching.

The account repeats the shut doors, Jesus' standing in the midst and His peace greeting, but now dates it after eight days and explicitly includes Thomas. The two appearances are deliberately parallel and distinct; the earlier Thomas absence and later presence are not collapsed into one evening.

Both passages offer bodily verification by seeing and touch. John directs Thomas's finger and hand toward hands and side; Luke addresses the group about hands, feet, flesh and bones. The invitations, body parts and audiences differ, and neither is used to invent an unreported completed touch.

Thomas addresses Jesus as my Lord and my God; the prologue identifies the Word as with God and as God. The confession and opening declaration form a concrete deity-language connection within the Gospel, without replacing either passage's actual speaker, personal address or formulation.

Jesus blesses those who believe without having seen; the epistle describes readers who have not seen Him yet love, believe and rejoice, receiving faith's saving outcome. Both explicitly relate faith to the absence of physical sight, with a beatitude and a pastoral description as different forms of the teaching.

Both closing notices say Jesus did more than the written account records. John 20 specifically names other signs before disciples; John 21 gives the broader things-done statement and the world-and-books expression. The selection notices do not verify an invented list of unwritten acts or literalize the book-capacity rhetoric.

Both passages explain writing in relation to the Son, belief in His name and eternal life. The Gospel gives a belief-and-life purpose for its written signs; the epistle writes to believers so they may know they have life. Those related purposes remain distinct rather than making their audiences and exact wording identical.

The risen-Jesus scene is located at the Sea of Tiberias; the earlier narrative expressly identifies the Sea of Galilee as the Sea of Tiberias. This is a direct same-book place-name clarification, not a claim that the earlier crossing or feeding and the later fishing appearance are one event.

John includes the sons of Zebedee among this fishing company; Mark names James and John as Zebedee's sons in the earlier boat-and-calling scene. The reference clarifies the family designation without identifying John's two unnamed companions or automatically assigning the beloved-disciple description to one named son.

Both fishing narratives begin with a fruitless night's work before a Jesus-directed abundant catch. John records Peter's decision and the group's unsuccessful night after the resurrection; Luke gives Simon's report of the night's labor before obeying the command. The different settings and stages of discipleship are not combined.

Both scenes present the risen Jesus in view without immediate recognition: the disciples see Him on the shore and Mary sees Him near the tomb. John states nonrecognition without naming the same cause in either scene, so distance, light or altered appearance is not supplied as an explanation.

The risen Jesus asks His followers about food in both scenes. John gives the shore-to-boat fish question and their No; Luke gives a request for something to eat, broiled fish and His explicit eating. The different answers, places and food actions are retained rather than made one meal.

Both accounts give Jesus' command, obedient casting and an unexpectedly great catch after failure. John specifies the boat's right side and difficulty drawing the net; Luke specifies deep water, nets beginning to tear and assistance from another boat. Their catches, equipment outcomes and before/after-resurrection settings remain distinct.

Both resurrection narratives distinguish Peter's actions from those of the beloved disciple. At the tomb the other disciple arrives first but Peter enters first; here the beloved disciple recognizes the Lord and Peter ties on his outer garment before entering the sea. The differing priorities and clothing sequence remain, and the unnamed disciple receives no added personal name.

Both great-catch narratives describe fellow disciples handling the fish with boats. Luke brings partners in the other boat and describes both boats dangerously full; John has the other disciples come in the little boat dragging the net after Peter leaves it. Boat roles, distance and the absence of a sinking statement in John remain distinct.

The charcoal fire recurs in Peter's story: one is in the high-priestly courtyard amid his denials, the other on the shore before the later love-and-flock charge. This is a specific repeated setting detail with contrasting company and purpose, not the same fire or a statement that John names who lit the shore fire.

Both narratives describe a great fish catch and its strain on the equipment. Luke says the nets begin to tear and two boats become loaded; John gives 153 large fish and expressly says the net is not torn. Number, net outcome and boat details are retained without an invented symbolic fish count or an identical catch.

Both risen-Jesus scenes involve food with the disciples, but the roles and recognition differ. John gives His breakfast invitation to disciples who know the Lord; Luke gives His request and explicit fish-eating while the group still struggles to believe for joy. Luke's eating statement is not added as an explicit action in John's invitation.

Jesus takes and distributes bread and fish in both scenes. The earlier sign feeds the reclining crowd with thanksgiving; the shore scene gives the same foods to the disciples after the catch. The recipients and scale differ, and the earlier thanksgiving is not inserted into a scene that does not explicitly repeat it.

The third-revelation notice follows the two narrated group appearances: the first-day evening without Thomas and the gathering after eight days with him. This relates John's count to those prior scenes without making it a universal count of every appearance or denying Mary's earlier encounter and other supplied Gospel accounts.

Jesus charges Peter to feed His lambs; the epistle's fellow-elder exhortation calls for willing care of God's flock under the Chief Shepherd. This is a concrete pastoral-care comparison, not identical wording or a new determination of the ambiguous more than these in Jesus' love question.

Jesus tells Peter to shepherd His sheep; the elders' charge in Acts tells Spirit-appointed overseers to shepherd the Church of God. Both entrust care of God's people through the shepherd-and-flock image. Individual and plural recipients and the stated appointing roles remain distinct rather than an identical commissioning scene.

The explicitly third love question and renewed feeding charge are compared with Peter's earlier life-pledge and Jesus' prediction of three denials. The triadic faithfulness-and-failure pattern is concrete in John's narrative. It does not make the three questions a newly supplied one-for-one absolution formula or introduce love-word distinctions absent from this English text.

John narrates Jesus' forecast of Peter's belt being tied by another and his being carried where he does not wish, interpreted next as death; the epistle says the Lord made clear the approaching putting-off of the speaker's tent. Both concern a Christ-disclosed death prospect, without adding a date, an inverted crucifixion, or proof that the epistle quotes this exact disclosure.

Both narrator explanations interpret Jesus' preceding words as indicating the kind of death: John 12 concerns Jesus' being lifted up, and John 21 concerns Peter's forecast. The recurring explanatory formula does not exchange the persons or establish an identical execution method from the two images alone.

Jesus earlier tells Peter he cannot follow now but will follow later; after the death interpretation He now directly commands Follow Me. This is a specific Petrine following promise and renewed summons, not a new calendar date or an assertion that every earlier inability has been explained in the same way.

John expressly recalls the disciple who reclined against Jesus at supper and asked about the hander-over. The earlier supper narrative records the beloved disciple's position, Peter's signal and the question. The retrospective formulation is fuller than the earlier Lord, who is it, and neither passage supplies the disciple's personal name.

Jesus repeats the personal Follow Me charge after Peter asks about the other disciple. The earlier command follows Peter's death forecast; the later one contrasts Peter's task with a conditional statement about the other's remaining. The refrain does not turn that conditional into a promise of immortality.

The narrator explicitly corrects the undying-disciple rumor by repeating Jesus' actual conditional words from the preceding answer. This is a direct quotation-and-correction relationship. The if is retained, with no claim that Jesus predicted the disciple would never die or that the rumor establishes his later biography.

Both narrative witness statements affirm the testimony's truth. John 19 describes the one who saw and bears witness so others may believe; John 21 adds writing and the plural we know. The recurring formula is compared without assigning an unrecorded personal name or settling a new editorial theory about the plural voice.

Both ending statements distinguish Jesus' wider activity from what the book records. John 20 specifically mentions signs before the disciples; John 21 broadens to other things and the world-and-books expression. The correspondence does not literalize the capacity rhetoric or establish particular unwritten deeds as verified facts.

deferred.reason: The other disciple's acquaintance with the high priest, conversation with the woman doorkeeper and bringing Peter inside were read in their full order. Other courtyard accounts do not reproduce this particular admission through an unnamed intermediary, and that disciple is not automatically identified as the beloved disciple or given a personal name.

Jesus' question whether Pilate's royal description is his own or received from others was read with the ensuing dialogue. Other identity inquiries do not establish this particular contrast of personal and reported knowledge; Pilate's motives or a new answer on his behalf are not invented.

Pilate's increased fear after the Son-of-God allegation was read with the next origin question. Other judicial anxieties, dreams or fear responses do not supply this scene's particular cause or confirm an unstated inner belief, so no general fear parallel is forced.

Pilate's refusal to revise the inscription was read after the chief priests' proposed change. General statements about irrevocable royal writings do not establish a parallel rule or motive for this particular placard; no independent counterpart to the reply is retained.

The instruction to bring some newly caught fish was read with the existing fire, fish and bread and Peter's subsequent hauling. Other food requests and the earlier crowd-feeding scenes do not supply this particular catch-to-breakfast instruction, and no generic serving or command-response link is added.

Peter's question about the other disciple was read with Jesus' conditional answer and the rumor correction. Those explain the same exchange rather than supplying a separate counterpart; generic curiosity or judgment passages do not establish Peter's motive or the other disciple's future.

review_notes: All 164 actual original John units in chapters 17–21 were read in source order: 26, 40, 42, 31 and 25. The proposal contains 158 supported source units, 161 pairs and 6 explicit deferrals. No extra continuation bodies occur in the assigned source chapter or verse fields.

Every retained target and its relevant scene or argument context was read from the exact pinned Saints cache. Target IDs, contiguous original ranges, full source coverage, duplicate directed pairs and self-target exclusion are verified before handoff. Original wording, divisions, gaps, IDs and continuation material are unchanged.

The prayer's Father-given name, people, words, glory, work, protection, unity and love recur in specific farewell passages. The comparisons preserve pronouns and scopes without equating every type of unity or resolving a new systematic account of preexistence, election or divine relations.

John 10:29 retains the supplied What-My-Father-has-given-Me formulation; Matthew 6:13 says evil while John 17:15 says evil one. Neither is replaced with a familiar alternative reading. Intercession for the immediate disciples is not expanded into a denial of the same prayer's concern for the world's belief.

The garden arrest retains Kidron, the group descriptions, Jesus' questions, the fall, Peter and Malchus, and the permitted departure request. John's I-am repetitions are compared internally without claiming a verbatim Exodus divine-name quotation or adding a Judas kiss that this account does not narrate.

The unnamed disciple known to the high priest is not automatically identified with the beloved disciple. Annas, Caiaphas, the high-priest questions and the later transfer remain in the supplied sequence. Peter's accusers, postures, denial words and rooster notice retain their differences from the other Gospels.

Trial comparisons distinguish reported allegations from narrator assertions, including the claims about wrongdoing, tribute, sonship, kingship and Caesar. Divine derivation of authority does not erase the greater-sin statement or name its otherwise unnamed hander-over. No external execution-law reconstruction is approved by the textual comparisons.

John's about-sixth-hour presentation and Mark's third-hour crucifixion are explicitly compared without a clock conversion. Purple and scarlet descriptions, cross-carrying by Jesus and by Simon, and different public or private stages remain visible without invented handoff points, extra scourgings or textile explanations.

The inscription texts, languages and attributed authorship remain as supplied. This Luke 23:38 unit does not include the three-language clause. Proposed editing of the inscription is compared with the actual Jesus-Pilate exchange as an accusers' formulation, not silently adopted as Jesus' verbatim speech.

Clothing comparisons distinguish four garment parts from the seamless tunic, the later lying linen from the separately wrapped face cloth, and Lazarus's still-bound wrappings. No folded-napkin custom, fresh medical explanation or universalized burial sequence is added.

Greek-OT Psalm IDs are exact: 21:19 for clothing lots, 68:22 for thirst and sour wine, 33:21 for guarded bones, 26:2 for falling assailants and 118:160 for true words. Psalm 33:21 speaks of their bones in the plural. Exodus 12:46 supplies possible Passover bone background without claiming a uniquely proved quotation source.

Zechariah 12:10 retains look toward Me because they danced in mockery and mourning, while John 19:37 retains look on the One whom they pierced. The connection is expressly qualified as possible citation background with a wording mismatch; the Old Testament target is not rewritten to match a different edition.

Resurrection comparisons preserve women's names and numbers as narrated, darkness versus risen-sun descriptions, initial body-removal assumptions versus later encounter reports, two seated angels versus Luke's standing men, the different messages, and invitations versus narrated contact.

Peter and the other disciple retain distinct arrival, entry, belief and later recognition roles. John 20:8's unstated belief object and the following not-yet-Scripture understanding are not collapsed. Thomas is explicitly absent then present; the proposed touching is not asserted to have been performed.

The target Mark 16:9–11 is part of the supplied bracketed longer ending. Its existing provisional source-limitation status is retained; this pair is passage review of the provided text, not new specialist or apparatus approval of that ending.

Jesus' breathing is compared with Genesis' creative breath as a qualified image, and forgiveness/retention with the separate binding/loosing wording as a bounded responsibility comparison. Neither comparison supplies a new ritual procedure or resolves all subsequent interpretations of the Spirit or the commission.

The earlier and later fish catches remain separate: nights, commands, boats, nets beginning to tear versus an unbroken net, 153 fish, and the after-resurrection setting are preserved. Peter ties his outer garment before entering the sea; no walking-on-water event is inserted into this scene.

The charcoal-fire recurrence is a literary setting link rather than the same fire. Bread-and-fish distribution and resurrection meals retain who asks, supplies, receives and explicitly eats. John's third group-revelation marker does not become an exclusive count of every appearance.

The three love questions and the feed/shepherd/lambs/sheep formulations remain as supplied English. More than these is not assigned a definite comparison object, and no fresh Greek love-word hierarchy, one-for-one absolution formula, inverted crucifixion detail or date for Peter's death is added.

The beloved disciple's supper reference, the conditional remaining saying and its rumor correction are explicit internal links. The condition is not changed into an immortality promise, and the testimony's plural we and concluding I are not assigned a newly verified editorial identity.

This is AI-assisted English passage review against the pinned edition, not an exhaustive concordance, independent human specialist review, fresh critical-text approval or live external-anchor verification.
